latin.2722: THESIS I. CHRISTUS non uno in loco pronunciat malam arborem non posse facere bonos fructus. Porro homines universi per naturam arbores malae sunt. Quippe in peccato nati sunt & concepti, & sensus ac cogitatio cordis humani ad malum prona est a pueritia, ut Deus ipse apud Mosem testatur cap. 6. Gen. Ac proinde ab hominibus, si sibi ipsis relinquantur, nullum opus procedere potest vere bonum & Deo gratum, & quod sit ad salutem alicujus momenti: sed quicquid homines absque Dei gratia, & solius naturae viribus cogitant, aut faciunt, quantumcunque exterius splendere videatur, semper tamen intus aliquid putre habet, unde simpliciter vitiosum redditur.
latin.2723: II. Verum eos qui per naturam arbores putres & malae sunt Christus gratiae suae efficacia bonas arbores reddit. Homines enim per Spiritum suum, a corruptione peccati repurgat atque sanctificat, efficitque ut veterem hominem exuentes, novum hominem induant, & fiant novae creaturae, neque amplius peccato, sed justitiae serviant.
latin.2724: III. Quod autem illi qui sunt eo modo Christi spiritu innovati, & facti bonae arbores, ac, ut quandoque scriptura loquitur, arbores justitiae, possint opera bona sancta & justa facere, & reapse producant bonos ejusmodi fructus, qui Deo placeant atque accepti sint, res ita certa atque evidens est, ut de eo nemo ambigere possit, quin communi Christianorum sensui renunciet, & verbo Dei omnem authoritatem tollat.
latin.2725: IV. Idem enim Christus, qui negat arborem malam bonos fructus facere, ex opposito affirmat bonam arborem facere bonos fructus. Apostolus vero docet [marg.: Ephes. 2.] nos esse Dei facturam, creatos in Christo Jesu ad bona opera, quae praeparavit Deus, ut in iis ambulemus. Et [marg.: Tit. 2.] Christum dedisse semetipsum pro nobis, ut nos redimeret ab omni iniquitate, & mundaret sibi populum peculiarem sectatorem bonorum operum. Quae certe absque ulla ratione dicerentur, si fideles a Christo redempti, & in Christo de novo creati, nulla opera vere bona facere possent.
latin.2726: V. Praeterea quomodo dici possent fideles ambulare secundum spiritum, & non secundum carnem: Ac spiritui & non carni serere: Item induti esse novo homine qui creatus est secundum Deum, in justitia & sanctitate veritatis, & facti Justitiae servi, qui membra sua exhibent arma justitiae Deo, si ab iis nulla opera vere sancta & justa procedunt? Aut quid aliud quam opera justitiae & sanctitatis intelligere possumus, per fructum illum de quo dicit Dominus, qui manet in me, & ego in eo, hic fert fructum multum? Joh. 15.
latin.2727: VI. Neque dubium esse potest quin illud vere bonum & justum sit, quod recte factum a Deo judicatur, & quod Deus ipse ad justitiam imputat. At fideles quos Dei gratia renovavit, faciunt quae Dei judicio recta sunt, & quae agunt divino spiritu impellente, ad justitiam ipsis a Deo imputantur. Ita 15. cap. lib. 1. Regum, David dicitur fecisse rectum in oculis Domini. Et Deus ipse in eodem lib. cap. 14. Regem Jeroboham per Prophetam increpans, dicit illi, Non fuisti sicut servus meus David, qui custodivit mandata mea, & secutus est me in toto corde suo, faciens quod placitum esset in conspectu meo. Et Psal. 106. Quod zelo accensus Phinees ad iram Dei placandam aggressus est, dicitur ipsi fuisse ad justitiam imputatum. Stetit Phinees, inquit Propheta, & executus est justitiam: & fecit subsistere ultionem: & reputatum est ei in justitiam in generatione & generationem usque in sempiternum.
latin.2728: VII. Et certe quis negare ausit Deum quaerere atque diligere ex toto corde, & ex tota anima, esse opus vere bonum sanctum & Deo placens? sed Dei gratia id praestat in ipsius populo ut Deum ea ratione diligat, juxta illud quod dicit Moses, Deut. 30. Circumcidet Dominus Deus tuus cor tuum, & cor seminis tui, ut diligas Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde & ex tota anima, ut possis vivere. Atque hanc Deus gratiae suae vim exeruit in Davide, qui hoc Dei beneficium agnoscens & celebrans, Psal. 119. sic de seipso testatur: In toto corde meo exquisivi te. Et similiter in Josia, de quo scriptum est lib. 2. Reg. cap. 23. 23. similis non fuit ante eum Rex, qui reverteretur ad Dominum omni corde suo, in tota anima sua, & in universa virtute sua.
latin.2729: VIII. Ac profecto qui pertenderent in fidelibus nulla opera vere bona justa & sancta reperiri, hoc ipso illos salute excluderent, & aeternis inferni ignibus adjudicarent. Nam sine sanctificatione nemo videbit Dominum. Et [marg.: Mat. c. 5.] nisi inquit Christus, abundaverit justitia vestra plusquam scribarum & Pharisaeorum, non intrabitis in regnum coelorum. Quinimo declarat Dominus arborem omnem quae non fert fructum bonum excindendam esse & in ignem mittendam, Matth. cap. 7. Item palmitem omnem, qui fructum in eo non fert, tollendum esse atque colligendum, ut in ignem mittatur, & ardeat, Joh. 15.
latin.2730: IX. Igitur opera quae per Dei gratiam a fidelibus fiunt, cum vere bona & justa sint, nec revera sunt, nec sunt appellanda peccata. Quis ausit inter peccata numerare Abrahami in filio offerendo obsequium, Josephi continentiam, Eliae zelum & fervorem, & Pauli constantiam atque alacritatem in exequendo munere a Christo demandato, inter tot adversa atque pericula; aliaque virorum sanctorum egregia facta, quae Spiritus sanctus in scriptura laudat, & in exemplum aliis proponit?
latin.2731: X. Tantum abest ut ista, & similia piorum opera, quae per Dei gratiam & auxilium praestant, inter peccata numeremus, ut illa a peccatis toto genere discrepare libenter agnoscamus. Siquidem peccata lege divina prohibentur: Opera vero quae fideles per Dei gratiam faciunt lege praecipiuntur. Peccata Deo displicent, & sunt ipsi odio & abominationi: Opera vero piorum Deus amat, & eis delectatur. Illa Deus severe vindicat: haec vero secundum suam bonitatem remuneratur. Illa obstant hominis saluti: haec vero inter media salutis locum habent, & sunt via ad salutem a Deo praeparata. Illa minime Deum authorem habent, sed pravam voluntatem daemonis & hominis: haec vero sunt Deo ascribenda & fiunt spiritu illius movente. Denique per illa profanatur & blasphematur Dei nomen: per haec vero sanctificatur atque glorificatur.
latin.2732: XI. Neque solum a peccatis manifestis, id est, actionibus per se malis & lege vetitis differunt bona fidelium opera: sed etiam ab ipsis infidelium egregie factis, quae speciem virtutis habent, & civiliter bona ac laudabilia sunt. Etenim in ejusmodi actibus infidelium, quibus virtutem aliquam exercere videntur, puta benignitatis, justitiae & temperantiae, substantia quidem actionis bona est, veruntamen actio simpliciter est mala: quia non procedit ab eo principio a quo manare debent actiones omnes vere bonae & sanctae, scilicet, a Dei amore: neque tendit in finem ad quem spectare debent eaedem actiones, nimirum ad Dei gloriam. Sed fidelium opera per gratiam Dei facta ad gloriam Dei tendunt, & ex charitate procedunt. Ideoque actiones illae infidelium, utut hominum judicio speciosae videantur, Deo gratae & acceptae non sunt: nec quicquam authoribus suis ad salutem aeternam prosunt. Sed fidelium opera Deo grata atque accepta sunt, & aeternae salutis remunerationem ab eo accipiunt.
latin.2733: XII. Sed quantumvis bona sint fidelium opera minime tamen perfecta sunt. Hic enim observandum est aliud esse opus vere bonum & sanctum & aliud opus perfecte & undiquaque bonum. Fidelium opera per gratiam Dei facta vere quidem bona esse asserimus. Verum negamus esse perfecte bona, & ita ut ipsis nihil omnino desit.
latin.2734: XIII. Quippe duplex in iis occurrit imperfectio. Nam primo bonis operibus frequenter adnascuntur peccata quaedam leviora, quae illa suo contagio aliquo modo commaculant, & sunt veluti pulvis quidam iis aspersus, quo nitor eorum non parum obscuratur. Sic inter precandum saepe animus distrahitur. In audiendo Dei verbo non raro alienae cogitationes irrepunt. In largienda eleemosyna oriuntur motus quidam diffidentiae, & nonnulla inanis gloriae titillatio. Et similiter quum pro Christo patiendum est, divinae gloriae zelo immiscet se aliquis gloriae apud homines affectus. Quae sunt veluti strumae quaedam bonis ejusmodi operibus adnatae, quibus pretium eorum deteritur & imminuitur.
latin.2735: XIV. Sed praeterea ipsi actus boni per se considerati, idque etiam in viris pro hujus vitae mortalis & infirmae statu maxime perfectis, multum tamen a summa perfectione deficiunt. Neque id tantum volumus pios homines in bene agendo non attingere perfectionem illam ad quam beatae mentes in coelo perveniunt: sed illos quoque multum subsistere infra perfectionis gradum quem lex rigide sumpta ab homine exigit, & ad quem homo ex prima creationis lege obligabatur.
latin.2736: XV. Nempe lex illa a primo homine postulabat, ut omni cum alacritate atque promptitudine, absque ullo torpore, sive renitentia Deo obsequeretur, & reapse primus homo, quamdiu integer mansit, tale obsequium Deo exhibere poterat: nec tantillum ab ea perfectione recessisset absque vitio & culpa, cujus se in Dei judicio reum constituisset. Quantum vero jam ab ea perfectione absint qui sunt per Christi gratiam renati, testatur cujusque eorum sensus & conscientia. Etenim quum legi divinae obediunt & bene operantur, id non faciunt sine magna difficultate. Prava concupiscentia, quae post acceptam Dei Gratiam in iis manet, quando divino cultui & aliis actibus lege praeceptis vacandum est, multum illis languoris & torporis injicit: quum vero mala vitanda sunt, propensionem & inclinationem in iis ad illa excitat. Unde fit ut in bonis aegre sequantur Spiritus sancti ductum, & in malis aegre avellantur ab illecebris peccatorum. Proindeque nec mala fugiunt, nec bona prosequuntur tanto cum ardore, atque ex tam puro Gloriae Dei zelo, quam lege exigente, homo integer manens id praestare potuisset. Et ita bona eorum opera legi quidem conformia sunt, sed tamen non juxta ἀκρίβειαν illam, quam lex ex prima sua institutione aestimata exigit, & secundum quam homo nondum peccato corruptus, opera sua legi conformare poterat & debebat.
latin.2737: XVI. At, inquiet aliquis, si Renatorum opera a perfectione debita deficiunt, simpliciter mala, non bona dicenda sunt. Nam actio bona esse, & simpliciter talis dici non potest, nisi in se habeat omnia quae ad moralem bonitatem actionis requiruntur. Juxta illud in scholis vulgatum, Bonum est ex integra causa: malum est ex quovis defectu. Ut difficultas haec solvatur Observant Theologi, in operibus, alioquin ex suo genere, & quoad substantiam bonis, duo genera defectuum notari & occurrere posse. Primum est quando aliquid ex requisitis ad bonitatem moralem actionis nullo modo, seu in nullo gradu eis inest. Ut, exempli gratia, quum opus non procedit ex debito principio, videlicet ex fide, & ex Dei amore: vel non refertur ad debitum finem, nimirum ad Dei gloriam. Alterum est quum omnia quae ad bonitatem moralem requiruntur insunt actioni secundum speciem, & in aliquo gradu, sed tamen non illo gradu, nec secundum illam perfectionem quam lex in rigore suo considerata postulat. Ut, exempli gratia, quum actio procedit ex debito principio, sed minus perfecto, id est, quum procedit quidem ex fide, & charitate, sed tamen ex fide aliquatenus infirma, & ex charitate eum fervorem non habente quem exigit legis ἀκριβοδίκαιον. Et quum refertur quidem ad debitum finem, sed tamen non cum tanta intentionis puritate quantam Lex ex rigore justitiae postulat.
latin.2738: XVII. Defectus prioris generis specificus est & essentialis & actionem aliqua essentiali perfectione privat. Sed posterioris generis defectus gradualis est & accidentalis & ab actione tollit perfectionem tantum accidentalem & individualem. Adeoque actus ille cui aliquid priori modo deest, ita malus est ut simpliciter bonus dici non possit: si vero solum posteriori modo ipsi aliquid desit, non desinit esse vere & proprie bonus, licet imperfectam tantum bonitatem habeat.
latin.2739: XVIII. Ad prius genus pertinent actus infidelium qui videntur honesti & ex virtute profecti. Non enim ex fide promanant, & ex Dei amore, nec etiam ad Dei gloriam referuntur, ut supra jam diximus, ac proinde non possunt inter opera bona & sancta numerari, & talia dici simpliciter. Actiones vero fidelium auxilio Spiritus sancti, & per Christi gratiam factae, ad alterum istud genus referri debent: siquidem non tantum bonae sunt ratione objecti, & quoad substantiam, sed etiam ratione principii & finis, quandoquidem ex charitate fiunt, & tendunt ad Dei gloriam. Ideoque ejusmodi fidelium opera Deo probantur atque accepta sunt, ut vere & proprie bona, & talia simpliciter & absolute loquendo dici debent: licet non omnimodam bonitatem habeant, neque parum a summa perfectione deficiant.

sections.title: Bad trees cannot bear good fruit
sections.pass_a: THESIS I. CHRIST in more than one place declares that a bad tree cannot bear good fruits. Now all men by nature are bad trees. For they are born & conceived in sin, & the sense & thought of the human heart is prone to evil from childhood, as God himself testifies in Moses chap. 6. Gen. And therefore from men, if they are left to themselves, no work can proceed that is truly good & pleasing to God, & that is of any moment for salvation: but whatever men think, or do without the grace of God, & by the powers of nature alone, however much it may seem to shine outwardly, yet always has something rotten within, whence it is rendered simply vicious.
pass_b: Thesis I. Christ says more than once that a bad tree cannot produce good fruit. By nature every human being is a bad tree: we are conceived and born in sin, and, as God himself testifies through Moses in Genesis 6, the human heart's every feeling and thought leans toward evil from childhood.

So if people are left to themselves, no work can come from them that is truly good, pleasing to God, and of any value for salvation. Whatever they think or do without God's grace, by natural strength alone, may look splendid from outside, but there is always something rotten inside it, and that makes it simply faulty.

sections.title: Christ makes bad trees good
sections.pass_a: II. But those who by nature are rotten & bad trees Christ by the efficacy of his grace renders good trees. For by his Spirit he cleanses men from the corruption of sin & sanctifies them, & brings it about that, putting off the old man, they put on the new man, & become new creatures, & no longer serve sin, but righteousness.
pass_b: Thesis II. Christ, by the power of his grace, makes good trees out of those who are rotten and bad by nature. Through his Spirit he cleanses people from the corruption of sin and makes them holy.
He causes them to strip off the old self and put on the new, to become new creations, and to serve righteousness rather than sin from now on.

sections.title: The renewed can and do bear good fruit
sections.pass_a: III. But that those who are in this way renewed by the spirit of Christ, & made good trees, &, as Scripture sometimes speaks, trees of righteousness, can do good holy & just works, & in fact produce good fruits of that kind, which please God & are accepted, is a thing so certain & evident, that no one can doubt of it, without renouncing the common sense of Christians, & taking away all authority from the word of God.
pass_b: Thesis III. Those whom Christ's Spirit has renewed in this way have become good trees, or, as Scripture sometimes puts it, trees of righteousness. They can do good, holy and just works, and they really do bear good fruit of this kind, fruit that pleases God and is accepted by him.
This is so certain and so plain that no one can question it without abandoning what all Christians commonly understand and stripping God's word of all authority.

sections.title: Created in Christ for good works
sections.pass_a: IV. For the same Christ, who denies that a bad tree bears good fruits, on the other side affirms that a good tree bears good fruits. And the Apostle teaches [marg.: Ephes. 2.] that we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God has prepared, that we should walk in them. And [marg.: Tit. 2.] that Christ gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, & purify to himself a peculiar people, a follower of good works. Which things certainly would be said without any reason, if the faithful redeemed by Christ, & created anew in Christ, could do no truly good works.
pass_b: Thesis IV. The same Christ who says a bad tree cannot bear good fruit says, on the other side, that a good tree does bear good fruit. The apostle teaches (Ephesians 2) that we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared for us to walk in.

He also teaches (Titus 2) that Christ gave himself for us to redeem us from all wickedness and to purify for himself a people of his own who pursue good works. All this would be said for no reason at all if believers, redeemed by Christ and created anew in him, could not do any truly good works.

sections.title: Walking by the Spirit and bearing much fruit
sections.pass_a: V. Moreover how could the faithful be said to walk according to the spirit, & not according to the flesh: And to sow to the spirit & not to the flesh: Likewise to have put on the new man which is created according to God, in righteousness & holiness of truth, & to have been made servants of Righteousness, who present their members as weapons of righteousness to God, if no truly holy & just works proceed from them? Or what else can we understand than works of righteousness & holiness, by that fruit of which the Lord says, he who abides in me, & I in him, this one bears much fruit? John 15.
pass_b: Thesis V. Besides, how could believers be said to walk by the Spirit and not by the flesh, or to sow to the Spirit and not to the flesh? How could they be said to have put on the new self, created after God's likeness in righteousness and true holiness, and to have become slaves of righteousness who offer their bodies to God as instruments of righteousness, if no truly holy and just works come from them?
And what can we take the Lord to mean, if not works of righteousness and holiness, when he speaks in John 15 of the fruit borne by 'whoever remains in me, and I in him: he bears much fruit'?

sections.title: What God judges right and counts as righteousness
sections.pass_a: VI. Nor can there be any doubt that that is truly good & just, which is judged by God to be rightly done, & which God himself imputes for righteousness. But the faithful whom the grace of God has renewed, do what is right in God's judgment, & what they do at the impulse of the divine spirit, is imputed to them for righteousness by God. Thus in chap. 15. of book 1. of Kings, David is said to have done what was right in the eyes of the Lord. And God himself in the same book chap. 14. rebuking King Jeroboam by the Prophet, says to him, You have not been as my servant David, who kept my commandments, & followed me with all his heart, doing what was pleasing in my sight. And Psal. 106. What Phinehas, kindled with zeal, undertook to appease the wrath of God, is said to have been imputed to him for righteousness. Phinehas stood, says the Prophet, & executed justice: & made the vengeance cease: & it was counted to him for righteousness from generation to generation for ever.
pass_b: Thesis VI. There can be no doubt that what God judges rightly done, and what God himself counts as righteousness, is truly good and just. Believers whom God's grace has renewed do what is right in God's judgment, and what they do under the impulse of God's Spirit God counts to them as righteousness.

So in 1 Kings 15 David is said to have done what was right in the Lord's eyes. In chapter 14 of the same book God rebukes King Jeroboam through the prophet: 'You have not been like my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me with all his heart, doing what pleased me.'

In Psalm 106, what Phinehas did in his zeal to turn away God's anger is said to have been counted to him as righteousness: 'Phinehas stood up,' says the prophet, 'and carried out justice, and made the punishment cease; and it was counted to him as righteousness from generation to generation, for ever.'

sections.title: Loving God with the whole heart
sections.pass_a: VII. And surely who would dare deny that to seek & love God with the whole heart, & with the whole soul, is a truly good holy & God-pleasing work? but the grace of God brings it about in his people that they love God in that way, according to what Moses says, Deut. 30. The Lord your God will circumcise your heart, & the heart of your seed, that you may love the Lord your God with all your heart & with all your soul, that you may live. And God exercised this power of his grace in David, who acknowledging & celebrating this benefit of God, Psal. 119. thus testifies of himself: With my whole heart I have sought you. And likewise in Josiah, of whom it is written book 2. Kings chap. 23. 23. there was no King like him before him, who turned to the Lord with all his heart, with all his soul, & with all his strength.
pass_b: Thesis VII. Who would dare deny that seeking and loving God with all one's heart and soul is a truly good and holy work that pleases God? Yet God's grace brings his people to love him in just this way, as Moses says in Deuteronomy 30: 'The Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your descendants, so that you love the Lord your God with all your heart and all your soul, and live.'

God showed this power of his grace in David, who acknowledged and celebrated it and said of himself in Psalm 119, 'With my whole heart I have sought you.' He showed it likewise in Josiah, of whom 2 Kings 23 says that there was no king before him who turned to the Lord with all his heart, all his soul and all his strength.

sections.title: Without holiness no one will see the Lord
sections.pass_a: VIII. And indeed those who would maintain that no truly good just & holy works are found in the faithful, would by this very thing exclude them from salvation, & sentence them to the eternal fires of hell. For without sanctification no one will see the Lord. And [marg.: Mat. c. 5.] unless says Christ, your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes & Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. Nay rather the Lord declares that every tree which does not bear good fruit is to be cut down & cast into the fire, Matth. chap. 7. Likewise that every branch, which does not bear fruit in him, is to be taken away & gathered, that it may be cast into the fire, & burn, John 15.
pass_b: Thesis VIII. In fact anyone who insisted that believers have no truly good, just and holy works would by that very claim shut them out of salvation and condemn them to the eternal fire of hell.

Without holiness no one will see the Lord. Christ says, 'Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 5). The Lord even declares that every tree that does not bear good fruit is to be cut down and thrown into the fire (Matthew 7), and that every branch in him that bears no fruit is to be taken away and gathered up to be thrown into the fire and burned (John 15).

sections.title: The good works of believers are not sins
sections.pass_a: IX. Therefore the works which are done by the faithful through the grace of God, since they are truly good & just, neither are in reality, nor are to be called sins. Who would dare to number among sins Abraham's obedience in offering his son, Joseph's continence, Elijah's zeal & fervour, & Paul's constancy & eagerness in carrying out the office committed to him by Christ, amid so many adversities & dangers; & the other excellent deeds of holy men, which the Holy Spirit praises in Scripture, & sets forth as an example to others?
pass_b: Thesis IX. So the works believers do by God's grace are truly good and just; they are not sins and must not be called sins.

Who would dare to count as sins Abraham's obedience in offering up his son, Joseph's self-restraint, Elijah's zeal and fervour, or Paul's steadfastness and eagerness in carrying out the task Christ gave him amid so many hardships and dangers? Who would count as sins the other outstanding deeds of holy men that the Holy Spirit praises in Scripture and holds up as an example to others?

sections.title: Good works and sins differ in their whole kind
sections.pass_a: X. So far is it from our numbering these, & similar works of the godly, which they perform through the grace & help of God, among sins, that we willingly acknowledge that they differ from sins in their whole kind. For sins are forbidden by the divine law: But the works which the faithful do through the grace of God are commanded by the law. Sins displease God, & are a hatred & abomination to him: But the works of the godly God loves, & delights in them. The former God severely punishes: but the latter he rewards according to his goodness. The former stand in the way of man's salvation: but the latter have a place among the means of salvation, & are the way to salvation prepared by God. The former by no means have God as author, but the depraved will of the devil & of man: but the latter are to be ascribed to God & are done by his spirit moving. Finally by the former the name of God is profaned & blasphemed: but by the latter it is sanctified & glorified.
pass_b: Thesis X. Far from counting these and similar works of the godly, done with God's grace and help, among sins, we gladly acknowledge that they are a different kind of thing altogether.

God's law forbids sins, but it commands the works believers do by his grace. Sins displease God and he hates and abhors them; the works of the godly he loves and takes delight in. Sins he punishes severely; good works he rewards out of his goodness. Sins block a person's salvation; good works are among the means of salvation and are the road to it that God has prepared.

Sins do not have God as their author at all, but the corrupt will of the devil and of human beings; good works are to be credited to God and are done as his Spirit moves us. Finally, sins profane and blaspheme God's name, while good works hallow and glorify it.

sections.title: Unlike the fine deeds of unbelievers
sections.pass_a: XI. Nor do the good works of the faithful differ only from manifest sins, that is, from actions evil in themselves & forbidden by the law: but also from the very deeds of unbelievers excellently done, which have the appearance of virtue, & are civilly good & praiseworthy. For in such acts of unbelievers, in which they seem to exercise some virtue, say of kindness, justice & temperance, the substance of the action indeed is good, but yet the action is simply evil: because it does not proceed from that principle from which all truly good & holy actions ought to flow, namely, from the love of God: nor does it tend to the end at which the same actions ought to aim, namely to the glory of God. But the works of the faithful done through the grace of God tend to the glory of God, & proceed from charity. And therefore those actions of unbelievers, however fair they may seem in the judgement of men, are not pleasing & acceptable to God: nor do they profit their authors anything for eternal salvation. But the works of the faithful are pleasing & acceptable to God, & receive from him the reward of eternal salvation.
pass_b: Thesis XI. The good works of believers differ not only from open sins, that is, from actions that are evil in themselves and forbidden by the law. They also differ from the fine deeds of unbelievers that look like virtue and are good and praiseworthy by civic standards.

When unbelievers seem to practise some virtue, such as kindness, justice or self-control, the substance of the act is good, but the act as a whole is simply bad. It does not come from the source all truly good and holy actions must come from, the love of God, and it does not aim at the goal they must aim at, the glory of God.

Believers' works, done by God's grace, aim at God's glory and come from love. So those acts of unbelievers, however impressive they look to human judgment, are not pleasing or acceptable to God, and they do their doers no good at all for eternal salvation. Believers' works are pleasing and acceptable to God, and he rewards them with eternal salvation.

sections.title: Truly good, not perfectly good
sections.pass_a: XII. But however good the works of the faithful may be, yet they are by no means perfect. For here it must be observed that a truly good & holy work is one thing & a work perfectly & in every respect good is another. We assert that the works of the faithful done through the grace of God are truly good. But we deny that they are perfectly good, & such that nothing at all is lacking to them.
pass_b: Thesis XII. Yet however good believers' works are, they are by no means perfect. We must notice the difference between a work that is truly good and holy and a work that is perfectly good in every respect.
We maintain that the works believers do by God's grace are truly good. We deny that they are perfectly good, so good that they lack nothing whatever.

sections.title: The first imperfection: lighter sins that cling to good works
sections.pass_a: XIII. For a twofold imperfection is found in them. For first there frequently grow up with good works certain lighter sins, which in some way stain them by their contagion, & are as it were a kind of dust sprinkled on them, by which their lustre is not a little obscured. So in praying the mind is often distracted. In hearing God's word alien thoughts not seldom creep in. In giving alms there arise certain motions of distrust, & some tickling of vain glory. And likewise when one must suffer for Christ, some desire of glory among men mingles itself with zeal for the divine glory. Which are as it were certain swellings grown upon good works of this kind, by which their value is worn down & diminished.
pass_b: Thesis XIII. Their imperfection is of two kinds. First, lighter sins often spring up alongside good works and in some measure stain them by contact. They are like dust sprinkled over the works, dimming their brightness considerably.

So the mind often wanders during prayer. Stray thoughts frequently creep in while we listen to God's word. When we give alms, stirrings of distrust arise along with a certain itch for empty glory. In the same way, when we have to suffer for Christ, some wish for glory among people mixes itself with zeal for God's glory.
These are like swellings growing on good works of this kind, which wear away and reduce their worth.

sections.title: The second imperfection: the good acts themselves fall short
sections.pass_a: XIV. But besides, the good acts themselves considered in themselves, & that even in men most perfect for the state of this mortal & weak life, yet fall far short of the highest perfection. Nor do we mean only this, that godly men in doing well do not attain to that perfection to which the blessed minds in heaven attain: but that they also stop far below the degree of perfection which the law taken strictly demands from man, & to which man was bound by the law of his first creation.
pass_b: Thesis XIV. Second, the good acts themselves, considered in their own right, fall far short of the highest perfection, even in those who are as perfect as anyone can be in the state of this weak and mortal life.

We do not mean only that godly people, in doing good, fail to reach the perfection that the blessed in heaven attain. We mean that they also stop well below the degree of perfection that the law, strictly taken, requires of a human being, the degree to which humanity was bound by the law of its first creation.

sections.title: What the law asked of the first man, and what the regenerate give
sections.pass_a: XV. That law namely demanded from the first man, that he should obey God with all eagerness & readiness, without any sluggishness, or resistance, & in fact the first man, as long as he remained upright, could show such obedience to God: nor would he have departed ever so little from that perfection without fault & guilt, of which he would have made himself guilty in God's judgement. But how far those who are regenerate by the grace of Christ are now from that perfection, the sense & conscience of each of them testifies. For when they obey the divine law & do well, they do not do it without great difficulty. Depraved concupiscence, which remains in them after God's Grace has been received, when they must give themselves to divine worship & to other acts commanded by the law, casts much languor & sluggishness upon them: but when evils are to be avoided, it stirs up in them a propensity & inclination towards them. Whence it comes about that in good things they follow the leading of the Holy Spirit with difficulty, & in evil things they are torn away with difficulty from the allurements of sins. And so they neither flee evil, nor pursue good with so much ardour, & from so pure a zeal for God's Glory, as, the law requiring it, man remaining upright could have shown. And thus their good works are indeed conformed to the law, but yet not according to that ἀκρίβειαν, which the law, valued by its first institution, requires, & according to which man not yet corrupted by sin could & ought to conform his works to the law.
pass_b: Thesis XV. That law required the first man to obey God with complete eagerness and readiness, without any sluggishness or reluctance. As long as he stayed upright he really could give God that kind of obedience, and he could not have fallen even slightly short of it without a fault that would have made him guilty before God's judgment.

How far the regenerate now are from that perfection, each one's own feelings and conscience bear witness. When they obey God's law and do good, they do it only with great difficulty. The corrupt desire that remains in them after they have received God's grace weighs them down with listlessness and sluggishness when they need to give themselves to worshipping God and to the other acts the law commands; and when evil must be avoided, it stirs up in them a leaning and inclination toward it.

That is why they follow the Holy Spirit's lead toward good only with difficulty, and tear themselves away from the lure of sin only with difficulty. So they do not flee evil or pursue good with the ardour, or from the pure zeal for God's glory, that unfallen man could have shown as the law required.

Their good works do conform to the law, then, but not to the strict exactness (ἀκρίβειαν) the law demands when measured by its original institution, the exactness to which man, before sin corrupted him, could and should have conformed his works.

sections.title: Objection: then imperfect works are simply bad
sections.pass_a: XVI. But, someone will say, if the works of the Regenerate fall short of due perfection, they must be called simply bad, not good. For an action cannot be good, & simply be called such, unless it has in itself all things which are required for the moral goodness of an action. According to that saying common in the schools, Good comes from an entire cause: evil from any defect. That this difficulty may be resolved Theologians observe, that in works otherwise good in their kind, & as to substance, two kinds of defects can be noted & occur. The first is when something of what is required for the moral goodness of an action is in no way, or in no degree in them. As, for example, when a work does not proceed from the due principle, namely from faith, & from the love of God: or is not referred to the due end, namely to the glory of God. The other is when all things which are required for moral goodness are in the action according to their species, & in some degree, but yet not in that degree, nor according to that perfection which the law considered in its rigour demands. As, for example, when an action proceeds from the due principle, but less perfect, that is, when it proceeds indeed from faith, & charity, but yet from a faith somewhat weak, & from a charity not having that fervour which the strict justice (ἀκριβοδίκαιον) of the law requires. And when it is referred indeed to the due end, but yet not with so great purity of intention as the Law demands from the rigour of justice.
pass_b: Thesis XVI. Someone will object: if the works of the regenerate fall short of the perfection they owe, they ought to be called simply bad, not good. An act cannot be good, or simply be called good, unless it has everything that moral goodness in an act requires, according to the saying common in the schools: 'Good comes from a cause that is whole; evil from any defect.'

To answer this difficulty, theologians point out that works which are otherwise good in their kind and in substance can show two kinds of defect. The first is when something required for an act's moral goodness is not present at all, in any degree: for example, when a work does not come from the source it should, namely faith and the love of God, or is not directed to the end it should be, namely God's glory.

The second is when everything required for moral goodness is present in the act in kind and in some degree, but not in the degree or with the perfection that the law, taken in its full rigour, demands. For example, the act comes from the right source, but a less perfect one: it does come from faith and love, but from a faith that is somewhat weak and a love lacking the fervour that the law's exacting justice (ἀκριβοδίκαιον) requires. Again, it is directed to the right end, but without the purity of intention that the law, in strict justice, demands.

sections.title: Defects of kind and defects of degree
sections.pass_a: XVII. A defect of the former kind is specific & essential & deprives the action of some essential perfection. But a defect of the latter kind is gradual & accidental & takes from the action only an accidental & individual perfection. And so that act to which something is lacking in the former way, is so bad that it cannot be called simply good: but if something is lacking to it only in the latter way, it does not cease to be truly & properly good, although it has only an imperfect goodness.
pass_b: Thesis XVII. A defect of the first kind concerns the act's kind and essence, and robs it of some essential perfection. A defect of the second kind is one of degree and is accidental: it removes from the act only an accidental, individual perfection.

So an act that lacks something in the first way is bad, so bad that it cannot be called good without qualification. An act that lacks something only in the second way does not stop being truly and properly good, though its goodness is imperfect.

sections.title: Where the acts of unbelievers and of believers belong
sections.pass_a: XVIII. To the former kind belong the acts of unbelievers which seem honourable & to proceed from virtue. For they do not flow from faith, & from the love of God, nor are they referred to the glory of God, as we have already said above, & therefore they cannot be numbered among good & holy works, & be called such simply. But the actions of the faithful done by the help of the Holy Spirit, & through the grace of Christ, must be referred to that other kind: since they are good not only by reason of the object, & as to substance, but also by reason of principle & end, inasmuch as they are done from charity, & tend to the glory of God. And therefore such works of the faithful are approved by God & are accepted, as truly & properly good, & ought to be called such simply & absolutely speaking: although they do not have every kind of goodness, & fall not a little short of the highest perfection.
pass_b: Thesis XVIII. The acts of unbelievers that look honourable and seem to come from virtue belong to the first kind. As we said above, they do not come from faith and the love of God, and they are not directed to God's glory, so they cannot be counted among good and holy works or simply be called such.

The actions of believers, done with the help of the Holy Spirit and by Christ's grace, belong to the second kind. They are good not only in their object and substance but also in their source and their end, since they are done out of love and aim at God's glory.

That is why such works of believers are approved and accepted by God as truly and properly good, and should be called good simply and without qualification, even though they do not have every kind of goodness and fall well short of the highest perfection.
